title: What Does SQF Certification Actually Mean?
summary: SQF Fundamentals, Food Safety, or Quality: what's the difference, and why do retailers need it? Here's what SQF certification actually means for a food brand.
body_markdown:
[Certifications](https://thefreshfactory.co/blog-categories/certifications/)


October 1, 2026


Most food brands know to look for SQF certification on a co-manufacturer’s spec sheet. Fewer could explain what that certification actually covers, which SQF program a facility is certified under, or why a facility certified for Food Safety and Quality (like The Fresh Factory) is making a meaningfully different claim than one that simply passed a Fundamentals audit. Here’s how to interpret a facility’s SQF certification and what to look for when evaluating a co-man’s credentials.


## SQF Certifies the Facility, Not Your Brand


SQF certification is a facility certification, not a product one. A manufacturer being SQF certified says something about how that plant runs, including its food safety systems, its quality management, and its documentation and traceability.


When you’re vetting a co-manufacturer, their SQF certification tells you the facility meets a rigorous, independently audited standard. It doesn’t automatically mean every certification your brand wants is already in place — that’s a separate conversation with the manufacturer’s[R&D](https://thefreshfactory.co/food-development/) or quality team about what’s achievable for your specific formula.


## SQF’s Certification Programs


Before January 2018, SQF certification was organized by three different levels. As of SQF Code Edition 8, certification instead is organized into distinct certification programs.


### SQF Fundamentals (Formerly Level 1)


The[SQF Fundamentals Program](https://www.sqfi.com/our-program/certification-programs/fundamentals-program) is a simpler, more straightforward entryway into food safety for smaller or entry-stage businesses and organizations. Focusing on implementation rather than documentation, the Fundamentals Code applies Hazard Analysis Critical Control Point (HACCP) principles in a scaled-down form. Participants in this program don’t receive a score — Fundamentals audits are instead evaluated on non-conformances and deficiencies.


The Fundamentals certification is not recognized by the Global Food Safety Initiative (GFSI), which is the reason most established retailers won’t accept it on its own.


### SQF Food Safety (Formerly Level 2)


[The SQF Food Safety Program](https://www.sqfi.com/our-program/certification-programs/food-safety-program) is SQF’s core certification and the one held by most food manufacturers. Food Safety is broken down into 10 industry-specific codes, from food manufacturing to storage and distribution, and it requires a full HACCP-based food safety plan, documented risk assessments, traceability systems, food fraud prevention measures, and corrective and preventative action processes. This is the SQF code that satisfies GFSI recognition and the level most retailer vendor requirements are written around.


Food Safety audits result in a score out of 100.


### SQF Quality Code (Formerly Level 3)


The SQF Quality Program **** is an optional add-on certification for production, manufacturing, packaging, and distribution businesses that already hold a GFSI-benchmarked food safety certification or equivalent. This certification helps businesses demonstrate their commitment not only to food safety, but to food quality and performance.


The Quality Code applies a HACCP-style, risk-based approach to quality, monitoring key process parameters, catching deviations from control limits early, and defining corrective actions to reduce variation, waste, rework, and consumer complaints. Facilities that are SQF Quality Certified have proven their ability to manufacture quality products in an efficient operation.


## What Exactly Does That SQF Audit Score Mean?


When a food manufacturer reports their SQF score, they’re referring to their audit score through the SQF Food Safety Program. Facilities are scored out of 100, and that score determines certification status: “Excellent” (96–100), “Good” (86–95), “Complies” (70–85), or “Fail” (below 70). Non-conformances found during the audit get scored by severity; a minor issue costs 1 point, a major issue costs 5, and a critical finding costs 50 points off the top.


A facility that just barely met the “Complies” standard at 71 and a facility that scored a 98 both technically hold the same certification status on paper, but they’re not the same operation. Asking a co-manufacturer for their actual audit score, not just proof of certification, is a fair and useful question — most won’t hesitate to share it if the number is good.


## Retailer Requirements


Most food retailers ask for GFSI certification, but GFSI doesn’t certify facilities directly. It benchmarks certification schemes and recognizes several, including[SQF](https://www.sqfi.com/) ,[BRCGS](https://www.brcgs.com/) ,[PrimusGFS](https://primusauditingops.com/primusgfs/) , and[FSSC 22000](https://www.fssc.com/fssc-22000/) . A facility can satisfy a retailer’s GFSI requirement by holding any one of these certifications, including SQF.


For a brand vetting a co-manufacturer, the practical takeaway is that a facility holding SQF Food Safety Certification has already cleared the GFSI bar that Walmart, Whole Foods, Sprouts, and most major retailers set.


## The Fresh Factory’s SQF Certification


The Fresh Factory’s facilities hold SQF Food Safety and Quality certifications, with a decade-long average audit score of 98 out of 100 for Food Safety. That means we’ve implemented a rigorous, GFSI-recognized food safety management system to protect consumers, brands, and operations. It also shows our commitment to improving product and process quality alongside food safety management.


For a brand evaluating manufacturing partners, these certifications serve as a proxy for something harder to see from the outside: whether a co-manufacturer is fully committed to food safety, product quality, and performance.
